segs.text: Module four, objective four. How the degree of ionization affects the renal excretion of drugs. After drug is filtered into the tubule, some of it can cross back into the blood, which is tubular reabsorption. For weak acids and weak bases, how much crosses back depends on two things: the p H of the urine, the fluid in the renal tubule, and the drug's p K a. The p K a is a property of the drug that, together with the p H, fixes how much of the drug is ionized.

card.m: reabsorption depends on: urine pH, drug pK<sub>a</sub>
pK<sub>a</sub> + pH → how much is ionized

segs.text: A weak acid or weak base exists in two forms at once, ionized and nonionized. Only the nonionized form is lipid soluble enough to cross membranes and be reabsorbed; the ionized form stays in the urine. The split between the two forms at a given p H is the degree of ionization. A weak acid is more ionized in alkaline urine, and a weak base is more ionized in acidic urine. So in more alkaline urine, more of a weak acid stays ionized in the tubule, less is reabsorbed, and its renal clearance rises. In more acidic urine, more of a weak base stays ionized, less is reabsorbed, and its renal clearance rises. Filtration does not change, because it is passive and does not depend on urine p H.

card.m: nonionized: crosses, reabsorbed   ionized: stays, excreted
degree of ionization: the split at a given pH
weak acid: more ionized in alkaline urine   weak base: more ionized in acidic urine
weak acid, urine more alkaline → more ionized → less reabsorbed → Cl<sub>R</sub> up
weak base, urine more acidic → more ionized → less reabsorbed → Cl<sub>R</sub> up

segs.text: For a weak acid, p H equals p K a plus the log of ionized over nonionized; for a weak base, the ratio is nonionized over ionized. When the urine p H equals the p K a, the log is zero, so ionized and nonionized drug are present in equal amounts. For a weak acid, each unit the p H rises above the p K a multiplies the ratio of ionized to nonionized drug by ten. For a weak base the ratio is turned over, so each unit the p H falls below the p K a multiplies the ratio of ionized to nonionized drug by ten. Neither line is on the equation sheet.

card.m: e.g. weak acid, pK<sub>a</sub> 5: pH 5 → 1 : 1, pH 6 → 10 : 1, pH 7 → 100 : 1 (ionized : nonionized)
e.g. weak base, pK<sub>a</sub> 9: pH 8 → 10 : 1, pH 7 → 100 : 1 (ionized : nonionized)
ratio of amounts: no units; not on the sheet

segs.text: Weak acids have p K a values of three to eight, and weak bases seven point five to ten point five. The ranges overlap between seven point five and eight, so a p K a alone does not always settle whether a drug is treated as an acid or a base. A drug's p K a is fixed, so in one patient it is the urine p H that changes the split between ionized and nonionized drug.

card.m: pK<sub>a</sub> fixed → urine pH changes the split

segs.text: The two factors that govern reabsorption are the urine p H and the drug's p K a. A trap option names plasma p H or the filtration rate, but it is the p H of the fluid in the tubule that matters, and filtration does not depend on it. Another trap swaps the p K a ranges, putting weak bases at three to eight. A third mixes up the forms: the nonionized form is reabsorbed, and the ionized form is excreted. Reabsorption of the nonionized form is one reason why, in objective two, a drug's renal clearance can fall below G F R: it returns part of the filtered drug to the blood.
